document.title: Usama bin Ladin: Coordinating our Efforts and Sharpening our Message on bin Ladin (Islama 07841)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
document.note: [Secret] Discusses coordinating with UN efforts and pressing Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and the Taliban to cooperate on bin Laden. It reiterates that the U.S. reserves the right to take military action and will hold the Taliban responsible. It notes the need for pressure before the Khost strikes become 'old news' and calls Saudi Arabia the 'cornerstone' of efforts. Excised.

events.description: US Embassy Islamabad cable recommends coordinating with Saudi Arabia and sharpening message to Pakistan and the Taliban on bin Ladin.
Brahimi meets the US Ambassador and explains support for a Tashkent meeting.
Taliban killed hundreds if not thousands of Shi'a and other non-combatants in Mazar-i-Sharif.
US strikes on Khost, described as a wasting asset.
Pakistan flew Saudi intelligence chief Prince Turki to Kandahar regarding bin Ladin.
US Embassy Islamabad cable recommends coordinating with Saudi Arabia and sharpening messages to Pakistan and the Taliban on bin Ladin.
Taliban killed hundreds or thousands of Shi'a and other non-combatants at Mazar-i-Sharif.
Brahimi met the US Ambassador and explained support for a Tashkent meeting.
Pakistan flew Prince Turki to Kandahar to press Taliban on bin Ladin.
US strikes on Khost referred to as a wasting asset.
Saudi Arabia decided to downgrade ties with the Taliban.
Karimov and Yeltsin discussed in Tashkent and agreed all factions should be invited.

US Embassy Islamabad cable ISLAMA 07841 (section 3 of 3) sent to State Department, assessing the proposed Tashkent meeting of Afghan factions and the Six-Plus-Two format and suggesting a New York Six-Plus-Two meeting.
Proposed Tashkent meeting where all Afghan factions could meet to discuss forming a broad-based government; the Embassy warns it could raise regional tensions.

key_claims: The US Embassy judged bin Ladin's presence in Afghanistan the most important issue and urged coordination with Saudi Arabia.
Mullah Omar appears strongly committed to bin Ladin and unlikely to be swayed by US or Saudi efforts.
Pakistan has the closest ties with the Taliban but had done little beyond flying Prince Turki to Kandahar.
Other Taliban leaders may be nervous, increasing internal contradictions.
The Taliban might hand bin Ladin to Saudi Arabia but not to the US.
Saudi Arabia could press the UAE and cut aid to pressure the Taliban.
The embassy suggested a pre-Tashkent six-plus-two meeting in New York.
